title: Simplified synthesis of oxidized phospholipids on alkyl-amide scaffold
author: Oskolkova, Gesslbauer, et al.
materials: through two reactions. First, an oxylipin (

steps.title: Boc-protect amino group
steps.instruction: Dissolve 2‑amino‑2‑deoxy‑1‑O‑hexadecyl‑sn‑glycerol (1) in dry dichloromethane, add Boc2O and triethylamine (TEA) and stir under anhydrous conditions until the reaction is complete (monitor by TLC).

steps.title: Phosphitylate Boc‑protected intermediate
steps.instruction: To the Boc‑protected compound (2) add bis(diisopropylamino)-cyanoethoxyphosphine and diisopropylammonium tetrazolide in dry CH2Cl2 under anhydrous conditions; stir until quantitative conversion (confirm by TLC).

substeps.instruction: Extract the reaction mixture with an appropriate organic solvent.
Purify the crude product (3) by silica‑gel column chromatography.
Dry the isolated compound (3) and store it under argon at –80 °C (stable for ≥6 months).

steps.title: One‑pot synthesis of lyso‑amino‑PC
steps.instruction: In dry CH2Cl2, treat compound (3) with choline tosylate and 1H‑tetrazol; monitor the reaction by TLC. When complete, add tert‑butyl hydroperoxide (t‑BuOOH) dissolved in dodecane to oxidize to triphosphate (4) and monitor by TLC. After completion, add TEA to remove the cyanoethyl protecting group, yielding diphosphate (5); isolate (5) by solid‑phase extraction (SPE). Finally, add trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) to remove the Boc group, evaporate under reduced pressure and obtain lyso‑amino‑PC (6). The product can be used directly or further purified by SPE or C18‑modified silica gel.

steps.title: Activate oxylipin as NHS ester
steps.instruction: Dissolve the oxylipin (7) in dichloromethane, add N‑hydroxysuccinimide and EDC; stir until complete conversion (verified by TLC). Perform liquid‑liquid extraction with a MeOH/CH2Cl2/water mixture, discard the aqueous phase (removing excess EDC and NHS), and evaporate the organic phase under a stream of argon to afford the activated NHS ester (8).

steps.title: Couple NHS ester to lyso‑amino‑PC
steps.instruction: Combine activated ester (8) with lyso‑amino‑PC (6) in dichloromethane (or an equivalent solvent) and add triethylamine; stir, then evaporate the mixture under argon. Isolate the oxylipin‑PC conjugate (9) using a reversed‑phase C18 SPE cartridge.

steps.title: Purify oxylipin‑PC conjugates
steps.instruction: Load the crude product (9) onto a C18 SPE column and elute with a gradient from 70 % to 100 % methanol in water. For prostaglandin F2α‑containing conjugate (9e), use an ethanol‑in‑water gradient instead of methanol.

steps.title: Mass‑spectrometric analysis
steps.instruction: Dissolve each synthetic compound in 80 % methanol containing 1 % (v/v) formic acid (Fluka). Record spectra on an LTQ‑XL ion‑trap mass spectrometer at a spray voltage of 1.9 kV, capillary temperature 200 °C, capillary voltage 45 V, in positive‑ion mode scanning m/z 100–2000 (or 200–2000).

steps.title: NMR characterization
steps.instruction: Acquire ^1H NMR spectra on a Varian Unity Inova 400 (400 MHz) or a Bruker AVANCE III 300 (300 MHz) at 300 K, and ^31P NMR spectra on the Bruker AVANCE III 300. Report chemical shifts (δ) in ppm relative to tetramethylsilane.

steps.title: Test coupling solvents
steps.instruction: Perform the coupling of PGE2 with lyso‑amino‑PC (6) in various solvent systems: THF‑CH2Cl2 (1:1 or 2:1 v/v), THF‑MeOH (10:1 v/v), THF‑ACN‑MeOH (3:1:0.5 v/v/v), up to 10 % water in THF, or up to 10 % TEA (v/v). Using equimolar oxylipin and lyso‑amino‑PC gives ~50 % yield; using a 2‑fold molar excess of lyso‑amino‑PC yields near‑complete incorporation. Analyze the reaction outcome by TLC and mass spectrometry.

description: Alkyl-amide phospholipids 9a-9g were prepared with the goal of using them as anti-lipopolysaccharide (anti-LPS) and endothelial barrier-protecting compounds. It has been found that oxidized phospholipids with the alkyl-amide scaffold are effective anti-LPS compounds, demonstrating activity both in vitro and in vivo [19]. Additionally, they were able to enhance the endothelial barrier in quiescent lung endothelial cells and restore the barrier function disrupted by LPS, IL-6, or thrombin as tested in both in vitro and in vivo models [19]. In summary, the effects of alkyl-amide oxidized phospholipids were found to be identical to those induced by diacyl analogs, specifically oxidized 1-palmitoyl-2-arachidonoyl-sn‑glycero-3-phosphocholine [24,25].
